 © 2026 Yahoo. All rights reserved. NAPLES, Fla. — The LPGA concludes its 2026 season this week at the $11 million CME Group Tour Championship. As it plans for next year, the key to achieving growth centers on two things: collaborating with the PGA Tour and playing events in more network broadcast windows.
 "We're working to make sure we follow PGA Tour coverage because we benefit from their lead-in," LPGA commissioner Craig Kessler said Wednesday at his pre-tournament press conference.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The LPGA will have at least eight weekend TV slots on CBS or NBC directly following PGA Tour action next year, which is double this season's total. The LPGA's broadcast deals with Golf Channel, NBC, and CBS are tied into the PGA Tour's $700 million annual media contracts with those same networks and ESPN—although the LPGA receives just a small percentage of the rights fee revenue.
 Through the LPGA's Japan Classic Nov. 5-8, viewership this season across all networks was up 7% compared to 2025, but flat on Golf Channel, showcasing the value of the increased reach over-the-air networks provide. The U.S. Women's Open was the most-watched women's golf broadcast of the year with an average audience of 1.3 million on NBC when Nelly Korda won her fourth major championship ; the audience peaked at 2.1 million viewers. Total viewership across the five women's majors was up 21% over last year.
 "When we show up in the right channels—when we're on network in particular—and fans have a chance to browse the channels, discover the LPGA and say to themselves, 'that seems interesting,' they tune in," Kessler said. "In fact, some of our numbers rival what Sunday Night Baseball used to do when it was on ESPN, and that's no small feat."
 The 2026 season was the first time the LPGA had no tape delays , as at least a portion of every round aired live on TV in the U.S.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Parlaying PGA Tour Plans
 In March, the inaugural Nanea Cup—a new $4 million event featuring LPGA pros and top collegiate amateurs—will air in primetime on Golf Channel directly following the conclusion of the PGA Tour's $25 million Players Championship's third and final rounds on the weekend. NBC airs the tournament broadcasts and Golf Channel airs its Live From The Players post-match show each day.
 "We're all after the same goal, which is growing the game and providing more exposure to people around the world, and that lends itself to collaboration," Kessler said. "In fact, our team right now is meeting with folks at the Golf Channel to make sure we lock in as many slots as we can that help us benefit from the lead-in."
 Kessler said he and his LPGA team have had "several conversations" with the PGA Tour "to make sure where we can collaborate, where it feels appropriate" moving forward. "I've gotten to know the leadership of the PGA Tour quite well over the last year and a half," he said.
